newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-FIS WITHDRAW OLYMPIC DOWNHILL THREAT.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-FIS WITHDRAW OLYMPIC DOWNHILL THREAT.

text.p: Alpine skiing's governing body, who threatened last year to consider holding the 1998 Nagano Olympic downhill races outside of Japan, said on Friday there was no risk of that happening.
"It was a threat, even a joke," said International Ski Federation (FIS) secretary general Gian-Franco Kasper in an interview before the Alpine world championships which start here on Sunday.
Kasper said that he had most recently mooted Korea as a possible venue but it was an empty threat.
However, he said the world body still had a "terrible fight" on its hands to get what it wanted.
The FIS and local Nagano host committee are locked in dispute over the starting point of the downhills.
The world body wants the start of the course in Hakuba, 50 kms west of Nagano, to be at 1,800 metres above sea level to include a particularly good jump and add length.
Organisers have said that would take it into a national park and are insisting on a start at 1,680 metres.

Makato Kobayashi, the director general of the Nagano Organising Committee, told Reuters in Japan that the start would not be changed. "We're just not going to move the starting point. That's it. End of story," he said.
FIS said last year that the inspections and test events staged on the projected course had proved the layout was too short and did not meet FIS minimum standards.
However, Kasper said on Friday that the modern and technically difficult piste was unquestionably the best available in Japan and met the standards.
"But we would like, although it's not necessary, to start higher up than we can at the moment."
Kasper said the FIS could not understand why recreational skiers were allowed to use the upper part of the piste but 50 Olympic downhillers could not race down it.
He said the FIS had promised "not to put in cables or anything. No starting hut, we would do it in snow. But they have all their ski schools and everything up there anyhow".

Kasper said the real obstacle was that the organising committee had agreed with environmental groups not to go into parks when Nagano applied for the Games and "a lot of people would lose their face" if they did so now.
There was better news on another sticking point.
The FIS official said that local organisers had agreed finally after much discussion to move the two combined slalom races to the same venue as the downhills.
"We had two working problems in Nagano," he said. "The first one was the combined slalom.
"We wanted to have the combined slalom in Hakuba where we have the downhills.

"The organising committee insisted on having it in Shiga Kogen which is perhaps three or four hours away but in the case of bad weather, and we know the risks in Japan of bad weather, we need to stay in the same place."
That is because if a combined downhill is called off, the slalom is usually staged in its place to prevent the day being completely lost to the weather.
If the slalom venue is elsewhere, this option is no longer available and two days are effectively lost.
"Finally they gave in," said Kasper.
"Since a week it is agreed that we can have the two combined slaloms in Hakuba on the downhill course."
The slaloms were originally scheduled for Yamanouchi village, which also hosts the giant and slalom events.
Yamanouchi had been reluctant to lose the combined events while Hakuba did not want to host more.
